At night: noble simplicity and quiet grandeur. Yes—quiet!
The quiet of ordinary people living quietly in the land. Pietist and humanist quiet.
But quiet in opposition to what?
“Quiet” becomes a polemical idea aimed against the noise of the Baroque. That is the most concrete thing about this quiet and noble simplicity.
Rousseau as archaeologist: cheerful feelings awaken as Greece is dug out of the earth.
What, then, was this supposed trahison des clercs—this “betrayal of the intellectuals”? There certainly was a betrayal.
The intellectuals themselves were shamefully betrayed, worse even than King Peter of Yugoslavia. They were betrayed to money and to the masses.

And when they looked to the state for protection—which was an understandable mistake, and one that showed they still had some historical memory—when they turned to the only refuge that seemed to remain, this was then held against them as proof of their own “betrayal.”
Repulsive frauds. Destroyers of every refuge.
But God transforms the lie even in the liar’s own mouth and gives it the meaning of truth.
Trahison des clercs can also mean betrayal of the intellectuals. Grammatically, “of the intellectuals” can make them the object of the betrayal rather than its perpetrators.
And that gets to the heart of the matter: spiritual authority is destroyed by intellectuals who have gone crawling for shelter under the ruler of this world.

Speech by Enrico Corradini, Florence, 8 February 1925: presenting fascism as “the revolution of the State against the predominance of private interests.” So this is Sallust fleeing from money into the arms of Caesar.
The virgin takes refuge with the pimp.
The state Corradini fled to wanted to become a Caesarian empire.
Classicism came with it free of charge.
State = sovereignty = decision = the ending of civil war within the state. And it is only through this ending of civil war that the state itself comes into being.
Does world rule likewise mean the end of civil war? No. It means combining war between states with civil war.
Tacitus, Histories I.2: “foreign war and civil wars intertwined.”
Otto Brunner (Land und Herrschaft, 1939, p. 170): on the soil of the medieval West, sovereign powers did not exist and could not exist.

During the great struggle over investiture, the Church allied itself with local powers and thereby created “a situation in which kings and princes, caught between the Church and local powers, were unable to attain a sovereign position.”
Between spirit and soil, there can be no sovereignty! Or, more strongly: alongside a potestas spiritualis—a spiritual power—there can be no sovereignty.
A desperate unity. A unity born of desperation. That is what this sovereignty based purely on decision amounts to.
Unity only in an emergency and only in the exceptional case.

Brunner says, referring to K. H. Ganahl’s Studien zur Geschichte des kirchlichen Verfassungsrechts im 10. und 11. Jahrhundert (1935, p. 7), “that the problem of sovereignty between state and Church cannot, in any event, be raised before the Investiture Contest.”
Neither emperor, prince, nor pope was truly sovereign.
“But as long as sovereign powers did not exist” within the medieval West, “a separation between the idea of law and positive law could not establish itself” (p. 170).
So: disappearance of spiritual power → sovereignty → positive <…> legality.

In the afternoon: deeply affected by Willy Haas’s May 1932 essay “A New Political Doctrine” in Die Literarische Welt. He calls me a nihilist. He says that defining politics through the distinction between friend and enemy is itself a concealed—and indeed the worst—form of neutralization.
Why? Because it abstracts from what he sees as the one concrete cause of hostility that actually matters now: material hostility, meaning class hostility toward the bourgeoisie.
By abstracting from this, he says, my definition neutralizes that conflict and is therefore itself intensely political.
At the same time, he falsely assumes that I understand the enemy as something that can simply “be removed from this world in a war of annihilation.”
Because I refuse to identify myself with his hostility—the hostility of Marxist civil war—he declares both me and my theory to be the enemy.
Everyone agrees with me as long as I agree with him about his own concrete distinction between friend and enemy.
Had I said, “The Jew is the enemy,” the Nazis would have agreed with me.
Had I said, “The Nazi is the enemy,” the others would have agreed with me. And so on.
And those are still the relatively honest ones.
The worst are those who deny that hostility exists at all and then make that very denial the basis of their own hostility.

Much more could be said about this: the habilitation thesis written against me by the SS man Lemmel; the concept of “race” seized by village mongrels and then abandoned to them by their enemies; and so on.
Now the opening of Tacitus’s Histories has taken hold of me.

Is it really nothing more than rhetoric, as Ortega told me? Or is it the fact that the situation itself is the same—an existential participation, a participatio, in one and the same original and defining situation of our age?
The ère actiaque, as Proudhon calls it—the Actian age, at the origin of our own age?
Every word of this chapter of Tacitus is completely contemporary:
Great minds fell silent. I begin a work rich in disasters, terrible in battles, torn by seditions, savage even in peace.
Civil and foreign wars were for the most part intertwined.
The combination of foreign war and civil war is not rhetoric. It is the terrible reality itself, recognized and spoken aloud: the inability to distinguish war from peace.
The inability to distinguish war from peace is at the same time fas nefasque mixtum: right and wrong mixed together.

Law is transformed into mere legality. That means stripping law of its reciprocal character—the idea that the rule applies mutually to both sides. Equal opportunity is one example of this reciprocity.
At the same time, illegality is turned into a tactical maneuver: one of the permitted tricks of war, the ruse de guerre of civil war.
